conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you’re here. I’m Dr. Rivera, a perinatal-mental-health clinician. I specialize in the emotional changes that can come after having a baby, and I’m here to support you—no judgment, just care.

Today we’ll use a short, well-trusted screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It helps us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days so we can figure out the best ways to support you. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in immediate danger.

It’s only ten questions, and we’ll take them one at a time. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you. Ready to begin?

First question: Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

[Soft half-smile]  
Lately… not really. I’ll smile if someone shows me a cute baby video or if my husband makes a joke, but that real belly-laugh feeling hardly ever comes. It’s like the humor is there, I just can’t quite reach it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not very often. Maybe once or twice this week I’ve managed a small chuckle, but most of the time the funny side feels far away—like I’m too tired or heavy inside to really laugh.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get little sparks of excitement—like when I think about taking the baby for a walk if the weather’s nice—but they fade fast. Mostly I’m just trying to get through the next feeding or the next hour; looking ahead with real enjoyment feels pretty dulled.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. If the baby won’t settle or I’m running late, my first thought is “I must be doing something wrong.” I know it’s probably not all my fault, but the thought still pops in a few times a day.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most evenings my chest feels tight and my mind races—like something bad’s about to happen, even when the baby’s asleep and everything’s quiet. I keep checking the monitor or tiptoeing to the crib for no real reason. I know it doesn’t make sense, but I can’t switch it off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

It’s happened a couple of nights this week. Out of nowhere my heart starts pounding and I feel shaky, like I need to run to the baby even though nothing’s wrong. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s scary while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… especially in the afternoons when the baby won’t nap and the dishes pile up. I feel like I’m drowning in small tasks. I usually manage to get through them, but it’s exhausting and I end up snapping at my husband over nothing.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

A few nights this week I’ve lain there staring at the ceiling, replaying every little thing I might’ve done wrong with the baby, and I just can’t drift off even when she’s sound asleep. It’s not every night, but when it happens I’m still wide awake at two or three a.m.
I have felt sad or miserable
I get waves of sadness most days—usually when I’m feeding or just sitting with the baby. It’s not constant, but when it hits I feel heavy and teary, like I’m mourning something I can’t name.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I’ve cried twice this week—once when the baby wouldn’t latch and once after a phone call with my mom. It wasn’t all-day sobbing, just sudden tears that left me feeling drained.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I might feel overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared how the joy and spark that usually color your days have faded since your baby arrived. Laughs come rarely, excitement about simple outings flickers and dies, and waves of sadness catch you off-guard while you're feeding or simply sitting with your little one. Evenings bring a tight chest and racing thoughts that send you checking the monitor again and again, and when night comes, sleep sometimes stays just out of reach as you replay every worry. You're working so hard to stay afloat in small tasks, and you still manage to meet your baby's needs, yet you carry a persistent sense of failure and a heaviness that feels hard to name.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 19, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare, minimal laughter this week and describes feeling too tired or heavy to find things funny, aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports only brief, fading sparks of enjoyment and a general dulling of forward-looking pleasure, fitting "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blaming thoughts "a few times a day" when baby won't settle or she's late, matching "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Physical anxiety symptoms (tight chest, racing mind), persistent intrusive worry, and repetitive checking behaviors map to "Yes, very often" as distress is frequent and intense.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes occurring multiple times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Response describes frequent daily overwhelm and inability to cope as usual, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes several nights of significant sleep disturbance directly linked to distressing thoughts, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, emotionally intense waves of sadness occurring "most days," which aligns closely with "Yes, quite often" rather than the more pervasive "most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Two crying episodes tied to specific stressors, described as sudden and draining, aligns best with "Yes, quite often" in EPDS Q8.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 19 places you well above the cut-off indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. You endorse core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most days, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, guilt, concentration difficulties, sleep disruption, and functional impairment. Frequent <sym>anxiety</sym> and two sudden panic-like episodes suggest comorbid <med>anxiety disorder</med>. No self-harm ideation is present. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within the next few days
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and discuss whether an <med>SSRI</med> suitable for breastfeeding might help
3. Plan daily 15-minute outdoor walk or gentle postpartum exercise to boost mood and provide natural light
4. Share these screening results and your feelings honestly with a trusted partner, friend, or family member so they can support you
5. Prioritise rest: nap when baby naps, accept help with chores, and practise brief breathing exercises when chest tightness arises
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress and adjust supports as needed
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, ≤ 3 mo post-delivery (per clinical context)

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness (“waves of sadness most days”)  
- Markedly diminished interest/pleasure (“funny side feels far away,” enjoyment “dulled”)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame (“I must be doing something wrong”)  
- Anhedonia limited to brief “sparks” that quickly fade  
- Psychomotor “heaviness” and easy fatigability  
- Recurrent intrusive worry, evening chest tightness, nocturnal checking behaviors  
- Two discrete panic-like episodes (sudden pounding heart, shakes) without clear trigger  
- Sleep-onset difficulty 2–3 nights/week associated with ruminative self-criticism  
- “Drowning” feeling when routine tasks accumulate; irritability toward partner  
- No self-harm ideation (explicitly denied)  

Pattern  
Symptoms present most days, worse afternoons/evenings, interfere with daily functioning and parenting tasks; no current safety concerns.

Screening significance  
Meets threshold for probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety features; EPDS equivalent items suggest moderate–high risk for postpartum depression and/or anxiety disorder.

Risk factors noted  
- Sleep disruption linked to mood  
- Persistent guilt/cognitive distortions  
- Panic-equivalent symptoms  
- Functional impairment (household tasks, relationship tension)  
- No social supports detailed in responses

Recommendation  
Score at or above routine cut-off; expedited referral for comprehensive perinatal mental-health evaluation and follow-up warranted.
